Chikamatsu Monzaemon. The preeminent playwright of the Edo period who wrote for both bunraku puppet theatre and kabuki, crafting emotionally devastating plays that explored the collision between duty and desire, especially in lovers driven to double suicide.

Chikamatsu authored over one hundred twenty plays for bunraku puppet theatre, which was the dominant form during his lifetime. His scripts remain the core of the bunraku repertory even today. He pioneered the sewamono, or domestic play, genre, moving beyond historical and legendary subjects to stage contemporary stories of merchants, courtesans, and ordinary people entangled in ethical crises. His most famous work is The Love Suicides at Sonezaki, which premiered in 1703 and depicted the double suicide of two lovers forbidden to marry by class and family obligations. The play was so powerful that its premiere sparked actual imitative suicides, drawing government censure.

What distinguished Chikamatsu's work was his approach to character. His protagonist characters are driven by intense emotion and moral conviction, creating empathetic, psychologically complex figures rather than stock types—a major innovation in theatre characterization. He collaborated closely with the master puppet manipulator Takemoto Gidayū, whose chanting and musical accompaniment on the shamisen complemented Chikamatsu's dialogue and spectacle. The power of his scripts was such that they were equally performed in kabuki by live actors, demonstrating the theatrical power of his writing across different performance modes.
